title: Indigenous-led child care centre at 30 Christopher Drive
subtitle: Also: affordable housing partnerships, homelessness count preview, child care growth update, and a paramedic wage parity request.
overview: The committee recommended that Council authorize a lease of 30 Christopher Drive in Cambridge to The Healing of the Seven Generations. The group would run a licensed Indigenous-led non-profit child care centre there {{vote:m1}}. Staff said it would be the region's first such centre. It would be open to families across the region, who would apply through the OneList.

The committee also recommended that staff explore affordable housing partnerships with non-profit and private partners {{vote:m3}}. This follows an update on the Waterloo Region Housing Revitalization Plan. Staff described options for part of the Courtland Avenue site and for 140 Weber Street, and said they would return with fuller proposals.

Three items were received for information without a motion. These were an update on Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care growth, a preliminary overview of the 2024 point in time homelessness count, and the housing update. Further analysis of the count is expected in January 2025. A union delegate also asked the committee to pursue wage parity for paramedics. No action was taken on that request. The next meeting is January 14, 2025.

decisions.item: Indigenous-led child care at 30 Christopher Drive
decisions.detail: The committee recommended authorizing a five-year lease with two five-year renewable terms with The Healing of the Seven Generations to run a licensed Indigenous-led non-profit child care centre in Cambridge, on terms satisfactory to the Regional Solicitor {{vote:m1}}.
The committee recommended authorizing staff to explore partnerships with non-profit and private sectors that add or enhance affordable units, benefit existing tenants, or share costs {{vote:m3}}.

debate: On the child care centre, committee members asked how it would differ from mainstream care. The partner organization described a more family-like setting with knowledge keepers, language, traditional food and sacred fires. Councillors encouraged it to share learning with other child care centres.

Councillors asked about access to the centre. Staff said it will serve families region-wide, with an Indigenous-led section on the OneList. The partners said they would start small and hope to grow into broader, multi-generational programming later.

On the homelessness count, staff said the number was alarming but not surprising, and that the 2024 count was more thorough than 2021 because of work to reach hidden homelessness. Councillors asked about comparisons with other municipalities and about women and gender-diverse people who are hidden homeless. Staff said these would be addressed in the January analysis.

On housing, one councillor said public land should stay in public hands to keep long-term affordability. Staff said the options are meant to reduce rising costs and debt servicing, while still adding affordable units. They said an emergency shelter on those sites is not currently contemplated.

A paramedic union delegate said paramedic wages trail fire and police services and recent dispatcher wage gains, and that this puts retention at risk. One councillor said they were sensitive to the concern but that Council has to weigh it carefully.
